cards.title: 南非沙丁鱼大规模死亡，企鹅生存与渔民生计陷入两难

entities.name: 沙丁鱼（pilchards）
entities.explain: 一种小型海洋鱼类，被称为'海洋能量棒'，是企鹅、海豚、鲸鱼等众多海洋生物的主要食物来源

entities.name: Saldanha Bay
entities.explain: 南非西海岸的一个海湾，是重要的渔业港口

entities.name: 南非企鹅
entities.explain: 又称非洲企鹅，生活在南非和纳米比亚海岸，目前属于濒危物种

cards.summary: 自7月28日起，南非西海岸Saldanha Bay附近渔民发现大量死沙丁鱼漂浮海面，随后死鱼陆续被冲上开普敦附近海滩。数周内，从纳米比亚Henties Bay到南非东开普省Mbotyi，跨越2600公里海岸线均出现类似报告。沙丁鱼是企鹅等物种的关键食物来源，但关闭渔业让种群恢复将导致数百万美元的经济损失，使企鹅保护与渔民 livelihood 之间矛盾激化。
cards.relevant: 沙丁鱼是南部非洲海洋生态系统的基石物种，其大规模死亡可能引发生态链连锁反应，同时暴露了濒危物种保护与沿海社区经济生存之间的深层矛盾。
cards.context: 沙丁鱼是南部非洲海洋食物链的核心环节，近年来种群数量持续下降。此次大规模死亡事件横跨2600公里海岸线，原因尚在调查中，但可能与海洋温度变化、缺氧或疾病有关。南非企鹅作为濒危物种，高度依赖沙丁鱼为食，而当地渔民同样以捕捞沙丁鱼为生。
cards.source_analysis: 卫报野生动物栏目报道，该媒体在环境议题上通常持生态保护优先立场，关注人类活动对野生动物的影响。
cards.social_impact: 事件影响范围跨越南非和纳米比亚两国2600公里海岸线。若关闭沙丁鱼渔业，将直接影响数千渔民家庭生计，涉及数百万美元经济损失；若不干预，南非企鹅可能加速走向灭绝。

Then, in early August, more dead sardines began washing up on beaches near Cape Town. In the weeks that followed, similar reports came in from places across a vast area spanning 2,600km (1,600 miles) of coastline, such as Henties Bay in Namibia and Mbotyi in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa. Sardines, sometimes described as “the energy bars of the sea”, are a key food source for seabirds – including the critically endangered African penguin, which only feeds on sardines and anchovies – seals, common dolphins and other fish. Meanwhile, the commercial sardine fishery contributes billions of rands and thousands of jobs to South Africa’s economy. “We’ve never had an event of this scale,” says Dr Janet Coetzee, of the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, a scientist who specialises in small pelagic fish. “We are taking it very seriously. The minister got involved from the start, establishing a high-level task team comprising local management authorities, scientists, the fishing industry and municipalities to oversee a coordinated response.” Dead fish were sent for testing, and pilchard herpesvirus (PHV) was quickly identified as the primary culprit. The virus is specific to sardines and is not a threat to humans or animals who eat infected fish. While the source is still to be confirmed, it is likely that it was brought to South Africa via imported frozen pilchards used by the canning industry or as bait by commercial fishers. While herpesvirus is endemic in some sardine populations, naive populations are especially vulnerable to the virus. A paper published in 2016 did not detect PHV in South African sardines and cautioned against importing frozen sardines to South Africa for precisely this reason. There is a precedent. A PHV epidemic in Oceania, probably caused by importing sardines as feed for offshore bluefin tuna farms, in 1995 (and another in 1998-99) killed up to 60% of affected populations. Eventually the Australian population developed herd immunity, but it took years for the numbers to recover. Against this backdrop, the South African task team met in early September to chart a way forward. entities.explain: 英国具有特殊科学价值的湿地保护区，被誉为'英国的威尼斯'，是重要的野生动植物栖息地

entities.explain: 英国政府推出的机制，允许开发商通过缴纳费用来抵消建筑项目对环境的损害，以换取建房许可

cards.summary: 卫报独家披露，英国政府允许在诺福克湖区保护区建造近16000套住房的开发商税费被大幅削减，每套房减少数万英镑。批评者指出，削减后的税费远不足以覆盖缓解环境损害的实际成本。部长们称EDPs是促进住房增长与自然保护的'双赢'方案，但环保人士认为这是以牺牲保护区生态为代价换取开发。
cards.relevant: 该事件揭示了英国住房危机与生态保护之间的政策张力，EDPs机制是否真正能实现'双赢'还是沦为开发商的'通行证'，对全球类似生态补偿机制具有参考意义。
cards.context: 英国面临严重住房短缺，政府推出环境交付计划（EDPs）以加快建房审批。诺福克湖区是英国最重要的湿地保护区之一，政府允许在此区域建造近16000套住房，但要求开发商缴纳环境补偿费。卫报调查发现该费用已被大幅削减。
cards.source_analysis: 卫报独家报道，该媒体在环境议题上倾向批评政府开发政策，关注生态保护与商业利益的冲突。
cards.social_impact: 涉及近16000套住房的开发计划，每套房税费削减数万英镑，总削减金额可能达数亿英镑。若补偿费不足以覆盖生态修复成本，诺福克湖区湿地生态将面临不可逆损害。
cards.source_text: A new levy on developers to allow almost 16,000 homes to be built in the environmentally protected Norfolk Broads has been cut by tens of thousands of pounds per house, the Guardian can reveal. Ministers say the government’s environmental delivery plans (EDPs) were created to unblock housing growth across the country and are a “win-win” for development and nature. They allow environmental damage to protected habitats and species to be overlooked as long as developers pay into a nature restoration fund, which is used for conservation actions at a later date designed to address the impacts. Once the first instalment of the fee is paid, work can start immediately. Labelled by critics as “cash to trash”, the first EDP was published last week by the government’s nature adviser, Natural England. It allows 15,780 houses to be built within the Norfolk Broads, a heavily protected wetland network of 60 shallow lakes and winding rivers that is home to some of England’s rarest species. The published plan, which is open for consultation for 28 days, states that the developer will pay £2,675 per house – £42m in total – into the nature restoration fund to cover compensatory actions including fenland creation and restoration, a change in use of agricultural land to semi-natural habitat, catch-dyke restoration and deer management. But a previous draft of the EDP, seen by the Guardian, set the levy much higher. Ecologists said this was to properly reflect the realistic costs of mitigating the increased nutrient pollution from increased sewage pollution and urban run-off into protected chalk stream rivers – the Wensum, Bure and Yare – caused by the development. The fee was to be between £5,400 and £60,500 per house, depending on the scale of total nutrient pollution that the development would cause. The fenlands, marshes, bogs and mires of the Broads are a biodiversity hotspot, home to more than a quarter of the rarest wildlife in the UK such as the otter, cuckoo and fen orchid. Natural England acknowledges that the new homes will cause environmental harm in the form of physical, chemical, hydrological and biological damage to the habitats and rare species in the Broads from increased nitrogen and phosphorus pollution. But the EDP states that the payment of the levy and the conservation actions it funds “will materially outweigh the negative effect of the maximum amount of development on the conservation status of each identified environmental feature”. cards.summary: 印尼中爪哇省Ungaran山附近社区居民强烈反对政府重启地热发电项目，称该项目可能威胁当地水源和农业生计。此前8月，印尼能源与矿产资源部批准国家电力公司PLN推进该项目。这是印尼推动地热能源扩张过程中遭遇的最新地方阻力。
cards.relevant: 印尼是全球地热资源最丰富的国家之一，正大力推动可再生能源转型，但地方社区的反对凸显了能源开发与环境保护、社区权益之间的紧张关系。
cards.context: 印尼政府为减少对化石燃料依赖，积极推动地热发电。Ungaran山地热项目此前曾被搁置，2026年8月能源部批准PLN重启。当地社区担心钻井和管道建设会破坏地下水系统，影响灌溉和饮用水供应。

entities.name: Knepp Estate

cards.summary: 英国正经历迁徙昆虫数量激增，部分昆虫来自北非等遥远地区。7月一个闷热傍晚，生态学家Matt Phelps在Knepp Estate散步时听到一种英国本土生物无法发出的尖锐鸣声，随后与昆虫学家Graeme Lyons追踪调查。这一现象被认为是气候变暖推动昆虫向北扩张的结果。
cards.relevant: 昆虫迁徙模式的变化是气候危机的直接生物指标，新物种迁入可能重塑英国生态系统，既带来生物多样性增加的机遇，也可能引发生态失衡风险。
cards.context: 全球变暖导致昆虫栖息地向北扩展，英国作为温带岛国，近年来记录到越来越多来自南欧和北非的昆虫物种。Knepp Estate是英国著名的再野化项目所在地，生态学家在此长期监测物种变化。
cards.source_analysis: 卫报野生动物栏目报道，该媒体在气候议题上持科学共识立场，关注气候变化对生物多样性的影响。
cards.social_impact: 昆虫迁徙范围变化影响整个生态系统，包括授粉、害虫控制和食物链。新物种迁入可能对英国农业和本土生态产生长期影响。
cards.source_text: It was a stifling evening in July and Matt Phelps was out for a stroll, when a piercing, whirring noise stopped him in his tracks. As an ecologist, Phelps knows his fauna – and he could think of no UK creature that could emit such a sound. “It was like the classic sound effect of a cricket in a film, a beeping sort of little trilling sound,” said Phelps, who works at Knepp Estate in West Sussex. He returned with entomologist Graeme Lyons to track it down. But the sound, though incredibly loud, “seemed to be all around us … it was very ventriloquial”. The duo hunted for three hours. Night fell before they realised their quarry was, said Phelps, “literally below the ground where we stood”. Sure enough, in a crack in the parched clay they made the first identification of a Verge (or Bordeaux) cricket (Eumodicogryllus bordigalensis) in the British Isles. Once they announced it, other reports poured in. “It turns out there’s been this wave of them right at the moment when there was an enormous wildfire in Bordeaux,” said Phelps. “And it made you think: have some of these things fled the flames of southern Europe?” Verge crickets are just one of many “first sightings” of insects on the UK mainland this summer. It’s been an “extraordinary flood”, he said. And it’s not just the professionals who are finding them. Jackie Harmer, a retired secretary from North Cheshire, was one week into her new hobby of moth-trapping when she found an odd-looking creature native to the Iberian peninsula, Odice pergrata – a first for the UK. And David Cousins, a city trader who collects moths by night at his home in north Essex, opened his box one June dawn to find a white moth with bluish markings. “I just knew it was something really unusual,” he said. It turned out to be not just a new moth but “a completely undiscovered genus in Britain”. In north Africa and southern Europe it’s known as a spotted seal moth (Enolmis acanthella). Then there’s Olly Mkeown, 18, in Truro, who didn’t even leave his room to discover what were pronounced in August to be the UK mainland’s first breeding praying mantises. “I sat at my table doing some work and then one was crawling across my keyboard – and then I saw one on top of the chair and then I just started spotting loads all around the tables, chairs and then some on the walls as well,” he said. cards.source_text: A mass of floating weeds at Chia Lagoon, Malawi’s largest, is choking out waterways and livelihoods as farmers and fishers struggle to access fields and fishing areas. Seven months after the rainy season ended in Malawi, fields that once absorbed seasonal water at the lagoon are submerged, frustrating irrigated maize and rice production, according to farmers. Fishers also said it’s now hard to access fishing grounds as the weeds are blocking boat routes. “We have never seen anything like this,” said Ali Maulidi, who leads an association of more than 1,000 fishers in Nkhotakota district in central Malawi where the lagoon is located. “Due to waterlogged soils, matured cassava has rotted in some fields,” Maulidi told Mongabay in a phone interview. The lagoon, on the western shoreline of Lake Malawi, drains into the lake through a narrow channel. Communities said weeds and debris started collecting where the outlet begins in February, pushing the water back into the lagoon and flooding agricultural fields. Chia Lagoon covers 1,700 hectares (4,200 acres) and directly supports more than 7,800 households through rice, cassava and maize farming as well as fishing and bird hunting. The larger river network supports more than 55,000 agriculturalists. In December 2025, the lagoon was recognized as a Key Biodiversity Area because of its abundant bird, fish, plant, reptile and amphibian species. “We don’t understand what is happening here; but we’re worried because it’s greatly affecting us,” Maulidi said. Scientists too don’t fully understand why the weeds are accumulating now, but they have also suffered its impact. Early in the year, a team of researchers, including Tiwonge Mzumara-Gawa, an ecologist at Malawi University of Science and Technology, struggled to access parts of the lagoon for their study on land use in the watershed. The study hasn’t been published yet and it wasn’t focused on the weeds, but it could still help explain what’s going on. Mzumara-Gawa said the surrounding landscape is facing severe deforestation, farmland expansion and settlement growth. And farmers have encroached on the boundaries of the lagoon. “It’s like this place should be wetland and nobody should be cultivating here. But people are cultivating there and … contributing to all of this silt that’s coming into the marsh. So that is my greater theory,” she told Mongabay in a phone interview. cards.title: 评论：生物多样性信用市场不应照搬碳市场模式

entities.name: 生物多样性信用（biodiversity credits）
entities.explain: 一种新兴市场机制，通过交易'生物多样性单位'来资助生态保护项目

entities.name: 碳市场
entities.explain: 将碳排放权作为可交易商品的市场，核心是将碳排放简化为一个可交易的'吨'单位

entities.name: 可验证性（verifiability）
entities.explain: 指一项生态保护成果能否被独立、持续地核实和确认

cards.summary: Mongabay发表评论文章，主张生物多样性信用市场不应复制碳市场的做法——将一切简化为单一可交易单位。作者认为，生物多样性信用应以'声明能否被持续、独立验证'作为成功标准，而非追求一个优雅的单一数字。
cards.relevant: 生物多样性信用是新兴的生态融资工具，其设计方向将决定全球生态保护资金的效率和可信度。若照搬碳市场模式，可能重蹈碳信用'漂绿'和验证困难的覆辙。
cards.context: 碳市场因碳信用质量参差不齐、验证困难、'漂绿'等问题广受批评。随着生物多样性信用市场兴起，政策制定者和环保人士正在争论是否应借鉴碳市场经验，还是另辟蹊径。
cards.source_analysis: Mongabay评论文章，作者立场倾向于批判碳市场模式，主张生物多样性保护应注重实质验证而非市场化简化。
cards.social_impact: 生物多样性信用市场若设计不当，可能导致数亿美元生态保护资金流向无效项目，延误全球生物多样性保护目标。
cards.source_text: - The biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy the carbon market’s method of reducing everything to one tradable unit, a new op-ed argues. - Instead, these credits should be measured by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified, since their benefit cannot be expressed as simply as carbon credits can. - “A hectare of mangrove forest is not interchangeable with a hectare of grassland: pretending otherwise is closer to a category error than a measurement gap, and I suspect it is the real reason estimates of this market vary by a factor of 80,” the author writes. - This article is a commentary. The views expressed are those of the author, not necessarily of Mongabay. Here is the argument I want to make plainly, before anything else: the biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy carbon’s trick of reducing everything to one tradable unit, and should instead measure its own success by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified. Chasing a single elegant number, the way carbon markets did with metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e), is not what this field should be racing toward. It may, in fact, be the wrong goal altogether. The clearest evidence for this sits in plain view, in numbers that most people read as an embarrassment rather than as information. Every few months, a new market research report tells us exactly how large the global biodiversity credit market is. The trouble is, no two reports agree. One puts the 2025 market at roughly $90 million. Another, published around the same time, puts it at $7.1 billion. A third lands somewhere near $5.7 billion. These are not small rounding-off differences. They are the same year, the same broad market, and estimates that differ by a factor of nearly 80. Most commentary treats this gap as a sign that the data are still catching up with a young market, but I read it differently. cards.source_text: Critical theorists like Theodor Adorno may have overreached in claiming that all mass culture is mediocre, mechanized propaganda made to justify the status quo. But that doesn’t mean they were entirely wrong. Over and over we see even the most subversive art, literature, film, and music has a way of being tamed and Bowdlerized. Global mega-corporate industries don’t need to censor what they don’t like; they only need to buy it, rebrand it, or price it out of reach. So what? Why do we need challenging, independent art when we have endless entertainment? Is the concept a nostalgic, elitist, Eurocentric idea? Artists have justified the need for art since antiquity, with poetic and logical arguments of every kind. But Dada artists of the early 20th century broke ranks, building their movement on the insight that no defense could possibly mean anything when it came to art’s purpose, especially in the face of the technocratic slaughter of World War I. When the hyperrationalism of modernity led to mass death and destruction, the only humane response was to declare war on rationalization—to “destroy the hoaxes of reason,” as French artist Jean Arp put it. “For the disillusioned artists of the Dada movement,” the Museum of Modern Art explains, “the war merely confirmed the degradation of social structures that led to such violence: corrupt and nationalist politics, repressive social values, and unquestioning conformity of culture and thought.” Dada took a combative stance against, for one thing, the insistence that art justify its existence to win establishment approval. “All activity is vain,” declared poet Tristan Tzara in his 1918 “Dada Manifesto,” including the “monetary system, pharmaceutical product, or a bare leg advertising the ardent sterile spring…. The beginnings of Dada were not the beginnings of art, but of disgust” with the ossified culture of the “nice, nice bourgeois,” who would preserve at any cost “the possibility of wallowing in cushions and good things to eat.” “And so Dada,” wrote Tzara, “was born of a need for independence, of a distrust toward unity.” Such declarations aside, the movement was decidedly unified in its aims. “For us, art is not an end in itself,” poet Hugo Ball wrote. “It is an opportunity for the true perception and criticism of the times we live in.” This critique required new experimental techniques that deformed and repurposed the technologies of mass culture. cards.source_text: Many a foreigner has visited England and found it an unexpectedly surreal place. Some of that effect has to do with encountering familiar icons — Big Ben, double-decker Routemaster buses, Marmite — in cold, damp reality. More of it may be induced by the country’s simultaneously thoroughgoing cultures of normality and eccentricity, an endless source of inspiration for Monty Python’s Flying Circus and much other British comedy since. Yet England came relatively late to Surrealism, or rather, Surrealism came late to England. When the International Surrealist Exhibition opened at the New Burlington Galleries behind London’s Royal Academy in the summer of 1936, the Manchester Evening News decried it as “a travesty of everything that’s decent.” Naturally, the show was a smash hit. On display was work by artists including Pablo Picasso, René Magritte, Max Ernst, Alexander Calder, Giorgio de Chirico, Marcel Duchamp, Alberto Giacometti, Paul Klee, Man Ray, and Salvador Dalí, who turned up in person to deliver a lecture on “Authentic Paranoiac Phantoms.” In order to “descend to the subconscious” with a properly Surrealist literalism, he rented a diving suit and helmet from a local outfitter for his appearance. (You can see an actual image from 1936 here.) “The diving suit had extremely heavy lead shoes which I could barely lift,” he writes in his autobiography, as translated by Haakon Chevalier. “I therefore had to walk very slowly, leaning on friends who helped to move me, as though I were completely paralyzed, and thus I appeared before the audience holding two luxurious white Russian wolfhounds on a leash.” Only after he’d been talking for a few minutes did Dalí realize that “it would be impossible for me to deliver my speech through the glass window of my helmet. Moreover, I had been shut up in this thing for ten minutes and became heated from the exertions I had made in walking across the stage to reach my chair, so that I was dripping with perspiration, and felt faint and on the point of suffocating.” With the technician who’d screwed the helmet on in the first place nowhere to be found, his wife Gala and friend Edward James worked desperately to free him, eventually taking a hammer to the bolts. “At each blow I thought I would faint.” When Dalí finally emerged, the audience, having assumed it had all been an act, “was impressed by my really deathly pallor, which constituted the accurate gauge of that Dalinian dramatic element which never fails to attend my mo

The winner delivers a lecture and “may remain in residence at the Library of Congress for a short time thereafter, and will be expected to have some informal interaction with members of the United States Congress.” In the prize announcement, Acting Librarian of Congress Robert R. When critics begged her to tone it down after the 2013 VMAs, she dropped an acid Day-Glo vanity project with a Tibetan singing bowl instrumental and track titles like “Fucking Fucked Up” and “I’m So Drunk.” And for as long as we’ve demanded she turn it up a notch, she’s been trying to settle down. “We never get to see ourselves sleeping peacefully next to the ones that we love,” she lamented on the Miley Cyrus & Her Dead Petz outlier “Lighter,” hinting at where she wanted to go even amid the most dubious aesthetic swerve of her career: next to you in Malibu, basically. Whether she’s playing a party animal, a psychonaut, or a retro rock provocateur, the impulse driving Cyrus has always been more staid than it appears. She never wanted the party to last forever. On Bass Persuades, Cyrus’ follow-up to 2025’s turgid and Pink Floyd-“inspired” Something Beautiful, it appears she’s stopped in her tracks. Cyrus has gushed about the domestic bliss she’s found these days, happily sober and engaged to frequent collaborator Maxx Morando. At least Something Beautiful was a big swing-and-miss; Bass Persuades barely leaves an impression. Shuffling through the diluted glam-rock and disco-pop schmaltz that has weighed her down since 2020’s Plastic Hearts, Bass Persuades wonders why today’s “kids don’t want to dance,” then gives them absolutely nothing to dance to. No score yet, be the first to add. Cyrus has thankfully culled her collaborators post-Something Beautiful, but the cadre she’s kept could care less about building back better. Kid Harpoon and Michael Pollack, the same duo who helped churn out “Flowers,” return at steamroller force, flattening any and all signs of fun. “REDLIGHTS” shoots for ABBA and lands like something off their immersive museum’s waiting room soundtrack, coating Cyrus’ knockout timbre in an unnecessary robotic sheen. “Let’s Get Married” is yet another Bruno Mars-minded clunker, devoid of passion. cards.source_text: In this short video, Bill Hammack, an engineer and professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, details the extraordinary making and tragic ending of the British airship known as R101. Conceived in 1924 and first flown in 1929, R101 was intended to fly a regular route from England to India. Hammack uses archival images and his own deep research to trace the engineering and history of this remarkable vessel, which the British government planned as the flagship of a fleet that would criss-cross its then-sprawling empire. Those ambitious plans were abandoned after the airship crashed in France in October 1930, killing 48 of the 54 people on board. Hammack offers a riveting peek into a brief moment in aviation history – one ended for good by the crash of the Hindenburg in 1937 – when it appeared as if commercial airships might become a regular sight in skies across the world. The video accompanies Hammack’s book Fatal Flight: The True Story of Britain’s Last Great Airship (2017), which is available as a free audiobook at his website. cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 29 minute listen Forty iron rectangles, each one blunt as a piano key, rotate into a blurring fury that hides the eight-foot-long shaft at the heart of the flail chopper. I am perched atop several tons of iron, with 80 horsepower at my command. This part of farming is straightforward – even a mechanically challenged tree-hugger like me can manage to depress the clutch, shift into second, and ease the throttle forward. The tractor’s tall, deeply treaded tires churn, revolving into a smooth spin. Everything is spinning: fans, belts, alternator, the driveshaft, axles. I don’t understand the mechanism fully, yet the tractor and chopper and I are propelled forward across the knee-high whiskers of a coarsely bearded cornfield. It is Indian summer in southern Wisconsin. My wife and I and our young son live here on her family’s farm. Both of us are employed off the farm, but on weekends and many evenings I am an apprentice to my father-in-law, David. Today, we are taking advantage of a brief period of warm, dry weather. Winter is approaching, and I could be spending the day beside our woodsplitter – the gasoline-sipping, hydraulically heroic mechanism that makes it possible to put up several cords of firewood quickly each year – but that work can wait until the cool, sunny days of fall are shoved aside by the relentless spin of the earth into darkness, sleet, snow and frozen ground. The wall of tall green corn that stood here this summer has been transformed by fall and harvest. Little is standing after the field was stripped by a seed-combing combine. The mechanical tornado flails so loudly behind me: wailing against the air, grinding off the root-buttressed corn-stalk stumps, sucking up spent leaves and stripped cobs. In my wake, dry corn litter passes through the chopper like water compelled into frothy turbulence, falling again into an even, silent surface that hides so much activity below. No time to waste – the weather is expected to hold for another day, and I need to cover the field before the light fails this afternoon. Tomorrow, David will rake this chewed-up detritus into windrows and then come back for another round to bale them up. While it is good to leave some of this thatch on the field – to keep a roof over the soil and guard against erosion by wind and rain – we can afford to borrow some of this, which also makes good straw. cards.source_text: ‘Who wants a pistol? Raise your hand.’ At the Trail Dust Town theme park in Tucson, Arizona, visitors step out of their normal lives and into the city’s past. Or, more accurately, a funhouse mirror of the past that plays up the cowboy romance and tamps down the drudgery and poverty to cultivate a good ol’ time. Over the course of a day, the US directors Sue Ding and Sarah Garrahan capture visitors enjoying the park’s many attractions, including shooting games, live shows, rides and, of course, the opportunity to cosplay as sheriffs, outlaws and saloon girls in the old-timey photography studio. Throughout, park guests discuss what draws them to Trail Dust Town. Whether it’s movie mythos, a longing for a simpler, ‘less political’ era, or just the fun of escapism, there’s an undeniable allure in stepping into a romanticised past that never quite existed.

cards.source_text: One day, I’m posting here about how to address AI risks, the next, Daily Nous suffers from a “critical error” and goes down for over a week. Coincidence? Or evidence that the AI’s thought I was onto something? Yes I know it was the former… probably. What happened? Daily Nous and its server were hacked. This isn’t the first time the site has had problems. A month earlier, the site was subject to what looks like some kind of attack. And at several times over recent years, various types of malware have infected the site, causing assorted difficulties. I employ security and clean-up services, but they face an increasing number and variety of threats. Meanwhile, the site has been aging—it’s over 14 years old—with some of its components becoming outdated, mutually incompatible, and difficult or impossible to update. It had slowed down a bit, too. So when this last hack occurred, my technical consultant, John Hunt, recommended the site be rebuilt: taken apart, inspected piece by piece, problem elements fixed or replaced if necessary, and then put back together again, with even more security. “But what if we have to replace all of the pieces?” I asked. “Will it still be the same blog?” I wish I could say that the reason it has taken so long to get DN up and running again is that we were distracted by the metaphysics of blogular identity over time. But what really happened is that we just did what John recommended. And by “we” I mean mostly John. At the start of the process we thought it would only take a few days, but as it continued, various further issues were discovered that needed addressing. The result is not really a redesign of the site. It should look roughly the same as it did before (despite that we had to ditch the original “theme”–the code that gave the site its look). cards.source_text: This year’s Booker prize shortlist features some very familiar names – previous winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart are in the running once more, along with Pulitzer winner Elizabeth Strout and prominent British speculative fiction writer M John Harrison. Novelist and poet Luke Kennard and debut novelist Rebecca Perry are also in contention for the £50,000 prize, the winner of which will be announced on Monday 9 November. James, the Jamaican writer who took home the prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings, was shortlisted this time for The Disappearers. Set in Aids-era Jamaica, the novel centres around an attack on a group of queer men rehearsing John Herbert’s prison-set play Fortune and Men’s Eyes. Coming in at 640 pages, it’s the longest on the list. Stuart won in 2020 for Shuggie Bain; this time, he’s nominated for John of John, which tells the story of John-Calum Macleod’s homecoming to the Outer Hebrides. The book is an “ardent exploration of the half-lives of queer men condemned to love, pine and suffer in silence”, wrote Yagnishsing Dawoor in a Guardian review. Strout, who won the 2009 Pulitzer prize for her novel Olive Kitteridge, was previously longlisted for the Booker in 2016 for My Name is Lucy Barton, and shortlisted in 2022 for Oh William! This year, she is shortlisted for The Things We Never Say, which departs from the well-known cast of characters in her previous novels to introduce the history teacher Artie Dam, whose comfortable life on the Massachusetts coast is threatened by a secret, and by the realities of a changing US. Harrison, who judged the prize in 2022, is shortlisted for The End of Everything, a post-apocalyptic novel set in an unnamed Kent coastal town. The book, “as its title suggests, is about everything”, wrote Michel Faber in the Guardian. “It burrows deep into our psyches – into the psyche of our civilisation – and exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now.” The shortlisted books “took risks”, and they “could not be replicated by artificial intelligence – these are very human books”, said the writer Raymond Antrobus, who is on this year’s judging panel alongside the chair Mary Beard, Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, the writer Patricia Lockwood, and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu. Kennard made the list for Black Bag, his comic campus novel about an actor in his late 30s who takes a job involving attending lectures in a black leather bag as part of a psychological experiment. cards.source_text: In her second novel, 2009’s The Singer’s Gun, Emily St John Mandel tells the story of Anton Waker, a young man desperate to make a break from his criminal family. His plans are thwarted by his cousin Ari, whose hard-nosed talent for operating outside the law has become a way of life. A decade later in The Glass Hotel, a painting called Swan Dive that hangs in the lobby of the luxury retreat stands as a symbol of escape from a trap that is closing. You will not need to have read either of these earlier novels to enjoy Mandel’s seventh, Exit Party, though their loose intertwining of narrative threads will provide extra pleasure and a sense of homecoming for those who have. It is also interesting to observe Mandel’s evolution from a writer of quirky tales of offbeat protagonists to a novelist whose world-spanning, politically resonant narratives now attract a wide and devoted following. Exit Party begins five years into our future, in 2031. Ari Waker has just come out of prison after serving an 18-year sentence for the attempted murder by contract killing of her cousin Anton. Much has changed while she has been inside: a second civil war has devastated lives and blighted the economy, and the United States as such has ceased to exist. As the novel opens, the newly inaugurated independent State of California is celebrating the end of violence and the lifting of curfews. Ari and her flatmate Gloria have been invited to a party at the home of Gloria’s friend, Kareem. Ari has the feeling that she is meant to be there; she has experienced such premonitions before, and learned to trust them. Arriving at Kareem’s home, she has the sense that something strange is happening. A woman she’s never met before addresses her as Ibari – the name that is legally hers but never used. A painting disappears from the wall. Someone else talks of “extra people” and of the party being “a door that swings both ways”. “There’s something wrong with this party,” mumbles Kareem, before stepping out into the night and walking away. cards.source_text: One tedious aspect of Britain’s post-imperial melancholia is the number of amateur historians who would rather we stopped going on about our role in the slave trade. Isn’t it all in the past? Weren’t we the first to abolish it anyway? In April, the Reform party announced a new policy of halting visas to people from countries seeking slavery reparations from Britain. “The United Kingdom is not an ATM for ethnic grievances from the past,” the party’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, said. Unfortunately for those who would rather forget, the slave trade, as William Pettigrew argues in this grimly important book, can be found “in the depths of Britain’s grain”. Ninety per cent of the enslaved Africans transported to America went on British ships, and slave traders’ actions transformed Britain in ways that still resonate today. The erasure of this history began with the abolitionists, who quickly realised that identifying and shaming slave traders might harm their cause. They chose instead to argue that abolition would confirm Britain’s superior moral righteousness. Lauding abolition obscured what Pettigrew calls “slave gain”: Britain’s gigantic profiting from the trade. Wilkie Collins and Charles Dickens, in a jointly authored article of 1857, blithely suggested that the gains of slavery had evaporated “as the Arabian Wizard’s money turned to leaves”. Thus began a general tendency to downplay Britain’s role, offshoring slavery’s causes and effects to the Americas or localising them to port cities such as Bristol and Liverpool. Since April 2021, Pettigrew has led a group of nine academic historians identifying all the known investors – about 13,000 of them – who financed Britain’s brutal trafficking of 3.3 million enslaved Africans, of whom about half a million died during the Atlantic crossing. The traffic began in the 1560s with a syndicate of city merchants, naval and state officials. It soon earned royal approval, because of the role it played in humiliating the Spanish, increasing influence in the New World, establishing a foothold in west Africa, and enlarging the royal purse. After the Glorious Revolution of 1688, English slave merchants loosened their ties with the monarchy and embraced a free market. cards.source_text: AZ Chike’s No Rest for the Wicked is proof of the maxim that it takes 10 years to become an overnight sensation. The Los Angeles rapper stepped into the national spotlight in 2024 at Kendrick Lamar’s Juneteenth Pop Out, then turned up on Kendrick’s “Peekaboo,” on GNX, later that year. But anyone who did their research would have quickly figured out that Chike, who by 2024 had eight projects under his belt, had been rapping since 2013. His new album No Rest For the Wicked affirms why he was already “next before GNX,” as he raps on opener “Mercy.” Over 14 tracks, AZ Chike takes on the risky task of making a “something for everybody” rap album. Tracks like “God’s Favorite” and “Hateful + Grateful” steep the project in contemporary L.A. gangster-rap swing, while “Lamb Truck Keys” and “Negative” polish that raw aesthetic with a mainstream sheen. Elsewhere, he explores a pair of Tyler, the Creator’s synthy soundscapes, tackles sensual minimalism on “Need Your Love,” and heads to the trap on “Packed Up.” No score yet, be the first to add. AZ Chike recently told Bootleg Kev that Kendrick gave him A&R-like advice on sequencing the album, and it shows: The opening stretch does a particularly good job of showcasing the rapper’s versatility. He bursts out the gate on “Mercy,” gets flashy on “Lamb Truck Keys,” reflects on L.A. on “Skyrockets,” talks cash shit on “God’s Favorite,” woos a girl on “Need Your Love,” then swings for the fences with Tyler, the Creator on “Look Like My Mama” before the album’s first interlude. His progression across that opening salvo looks a little like the Vince McMahon meme tracking the wrestling promoter’s ascending degrees of euphoria. Southern California is full of snarling, artfully offbeat rappers in the lineage of the late Drakeo the Ruler, 03 Greedo, and Shoreline Mafia. AZ Chike is a card-carrying New West member, who uses his L.A. accent and lively delivery to splosh a variety of vocal tones over No Rest For the Wicked’s beats. He’s in his groove, channeling dog-on-a-leash fury on the album’s most impassioned moments, but knows how to rein it in and let melody lead him on the Tyler tracks and “Negative.” And he’s outright hushed on “Need Your Love,” where he and JMSN have the obligatory “for the ladies” moment without sounding banal or like creeps. items.title: Exit Party by Emily St John Mandel review – alternate visions of post-crisis America
items.summary: Is the price of stability necessarily the loss of freedom? Two possible future worlds are linked in the new novel from the author of Station Eleven In her second novel, 2009’s The Singer’s Gun, Emily St John Mandel tells the story of Anton Waker, a young man desperate to make a break from his criminal family. His plans are thwarted by his cousin Ari, whose hard-nosed talent for operating outside the law has become a way of life. A decade later in The Glass Hotel , a painting called Swan Dive that hangs in the lobby of the luxury retreat stands as a symbol of escape from a trap that is closing. You will not need to have read either of these earlier novels to enjoy Mandel’s seventh, Exit Party, though their loose intertwining of narrative threads will provide extra pleasure and a sense of homecoming for those who have. It is also interesting to observe Mandel’s evolution from a writer of quirky tales of offbeat protagonists to a novelist whose world-spanning, politically resonant narratives now attract a wide and devoted following. Exit Party begins five years into our future, in 2031. Ari Waker has just come out of prison after serving an 18-year sentence for the attempted murder by contract killing of her cousin Anton. Much has changed while she has been inside: a second civil war has devastated lives and blighted the economy, and the United States as such has ceased to exist. Continue reading...

Isn’t it all in the past? Weren’t we the first to abolish it anyway? Unfortunately for those who would rather forget, the slave trade, as William Pettigrew argues in this grimly important book, can be found “in the depths of Britain’s grain”.
